title: The Ruined Loincloth
sum: Jeremiah is told to buy a linen loincloth and wear it, then bury it in a crack of the rock at Perath. Many days later he digs it up, and it is rotten and good for nothing. The LORD explains: Judah and Israel were made to cling to him as a loincloth clings to a body, to be his people, his name, his praise and his honor, and they would not listen. So he will ruin their pride.

The rest of the chapter is a sermon in many pieces: a proverb about wine jars that turns into a threat of drunkenness, a call to give glory before the dark falls, a message for the king and the queen mother, and a long poem to Jerusalem about her shame. It ends with a question that has no answer in the chapter: 'How long will it be before you are clean?'
readings: Read as an acted parable
Jeremiah really took the cloth, buried it and dug it up. The sign is the whole of the sermon: what was meant to be close to God is rotting away from him, and the rot is Judah's pride.
Read as a vision or told story

Some readers, including many who think Perath is far away, hold that the journeys were seen in a vision or told as a story, since a trip to the Euphrates and back, twice, would take months. The point of the sign is not changed.
Read as literature
The chapter is arranged as a series of images that move from cloth to jars to a flock to a woman. Critics see an editor linking separate sayings under one theme of ruin and shame.

views.H: The poems about the king and the queen mother (13:18-19) fit the weeks after the first Babylonian siege in 597 BC, when Jehoiachin and his mother were taken away (2 Kings 24:8-16). The loincloth sign has no date. The Euphrates is the river of Babylon, so the buried cloth points to where Judah will be taken.
views.C: Scholars separate the prose sign-act (13:1-11), usually in Jeremiah's own memoir style or in the later editors' hands, from the poems (13:15-27) that may come from different years. Verse 11 has the language of Deuteronomy (compare Deuteronomy 26:19). The Greek lacks 'the LORD declares' in 13:11 and has a different set of words for 'praise and honor'.
views.J: Jewish readers have read the chapter as a warning to a people that took the LORD's nearness for granted. Whether Perath is the Euphrates or a nearer place is debated among Jewish as among Christian readers (see the note on 13:4). Rashi, in the Sefaria text, comments on 13:7 only that the cloth was not fit for anything.
views.X: Christian readers see in the cloth a warning against presuming on closeness to God. No New Testament writer quotes this sign. The picture of believers being 'clothed' with Christ (Galatians 3:27) uses clothing language, but it is a different image and not a use of the loincloth.
views.F: Some futurist readers see the northern foe as one still to come; most readers who hold this view treat chapter 13 as already fulfilled in 586 BC. The promise to bring the people back (16:14-15) is the part some read as still to come.

deep.b: Jeremiah's life is itself a message. He does not marry (16:1-9), buys a loincloth (13), watches a potter (18), smashes a jar (19), wears a yoke (27-28), buys a field (32), hides stones in Egypt (43:8-13) and has a scroll thrown into the Euphrates (51:59-64). Many scholars think ancient hearers took such acts as more than illustrations: a word spoken by a prophet was believed to help bring about what it announced, and the act was part of that. The question for a modern reader is whether the acts happened as told. The book does not say; it tells them as plain events. Some readers hold that every act happened, others that some of them are told as visions (as Ezekiel's often are). The Plain follows the text as written.

deep.h: The Greek in this chapter and the witnesses read
deep.b:
For the whole part (chapters 13-20) the Hebrew is the Leningrad Codex, 'the Greek' means the text in Swete's edition (Codex Vaticanus), and the two Dead Sea copies that survive in these chapters, 4QJer-a (4Q70) and 4QJer-c (4Q72), are read in the transcription of Abegg, Bowley and Cook (ETCBC dss). Where they survive in these chapters they agree with the Masoretic Text, apart from spelling and the few readings given in the variants. Rashi on 13:7 and 20:7 is cited from the text Sefaria prints.

In this chapter the Greek reads 'Euphrates' for Perath (13:4-7), 'pride' (hybris) for the Hebrew word for pride in 13:9, and 'the rulers' for 'the queen mother' (13:18, see the variant). It also lacks small things such as 'the LORD declares' in 13:11. Such small plus-and-minus differences, many of them names, titles and formulas, are all through the Greek of Jeremiah and are not listed as variants unless the sense changes.

echoes: Deuteronomy 26:19; Deuteronomy 10:20; Isaiah 51:17; Jeremiah 25:15-29; Jeremiah 2:2; Jeremiah 6:24; 2 Kings 24:8-16; Hosea 2:10; Nahum 3:5; Revelation 14:10

settings.by: The LORD, to Jeremiah, in a sign he acts out
settings.to: Jeremiah first, then those who saw or heard of it: the people of Jerusalem and Judah
settings.when: Undated; usually put in Jehoiakim's reign, before 597 BC, with a long gap between the burying and the digging up
settings.why: To show in an act what the people were to the LORD and what they have become: a garment worn close to the body that is now ruined and fit only to be thrown away. Judah's pride is the thing that will be ruined.
settings.readers: Exiles reading the book later saw in the Euphrates the river of their exile: what rotted there was what had been taken to Babylon.
views: Jeremiah went to the Euphrates twice, which would be a trip of many months.
He went to Parah (Joshua 18:23), a short walk from Anathoth.
The journeys were visionary, as in Ezekiel.

settings.by: The LORD, through Jeremiah
settings.to: The people of Jerusalem, who answer with the obvious ('Do we not know?')
settings.when: Undated
settings.why: To turn a harmless saying about full wine jars into a threat: the LORD will fill the leaders of Judah with drunkenness and smash them against each other.

settings.what: A poem of warning and shame
settings.by: Jeremiah, speaking for the LORD and weeping
settings.to: The people of Jerusalem; the king and the queen mother (13:18); the city of Jerusalem as a woman (13:20-27)
settings.when: Perhaps in the years of Babylon's rise, 605-597 BC; 13:18-19 may be from just before or after Jehoiachin's capture in 597 BC
settings.why: To call them to give glory to the LORD before it is too dark to find the way, and to say to the court and the city that what is happening is the fruit of their own conduct. The question 'How long?' ends with the city still unclean.
settings.readers: The exiles who read the poem knew its end; for them it explained how the king and queen mother came to Babylon.
views: The poem comes just before or after the first capture, and the king is Jehoiachin.
It is from Jehoiakim's reign and warns before the crisis.

title: Drought and the Closed Door
sum: The land is parched: gates droop, cisterns are empty, deer abandon their fawns and wild donkeys pant on the bare hills. The people pray, confessing their sins and appealing to God's name, and the LORD does not take them back. He tells Jeremiah not to pray for them, since fasting and offerings will not move him.

Jeremiah then complains that the prophets promise peace, and the LORD answers that those prophets were never sent and will die by the sword and famine they say will not come. The chapter ends with Jeremiah weeping, and a second prayer from the people asking the LORD not to reject Zion, with no answer given.
readings: Read as a liturgy

The chapter follows the pattern of a public fast in time of drought: a description, a prayer, an oracle of refusal, an argument, a second prayer. It may preserve how such services sounded in Jerusalem, and its refusal turns the service upside down.
Read as Jeremiah's own prayer
Jeremiah is the one who prays and weeps. The pleas for 'us' are his, and the LORD answers him, not the people.

views.H: The drought has no date. Dry years are named in 3:3 and 12:4. The prophets of peace of 14:13 are those Jeremiah met throughout Jehoiakim's and Zedekiah's reigns, and the sword and famine came with the sieges of 597 and 588-586 BC.
views.C: 14:1-15:4 is usually taken as a literary unit built from a drought poem, two laments and sermons on the prophets. Some critics see the prose of 14:11-16 as a later addition in the book's own prose style. The Greek of 14:9 has 'sleeping' where the Hebrew has a rare word, and 14:19b repeats 8:15 word for word.
views.J: The chapter has the form of a public fast-day service, and Jewish readers have noticed that the LORD's refusal turns the form upside down. The ban on prayer (14:11) is read as a verdict on this generation, not as a rule for all time.
views.X: Christians have read 14:13-16 as a model for the test of a prophet and 14:14 as a warning against those who speak without being sent.
views.F: Few readers find the drought itself still to come; futurists who read the prophets of peace as a type see in them the false teachers of the end (compare Matthew 24:11).

deep.b: Three times Jeremiah is told not to pray for the people (7:16; 11:14; 14:11), and in 15:1 even Moses and Samuel would not help. The bans come after the people have been warned many times and have not turned. The text does not say that prayer is useless in general: the book has Jeremiah pray, and later both Zedekiah and the people ask him to (37:3; 42:2). The point is that the day of judgment is fixed, and prayer cannot turn it aside. A reader may also note that Jeremiah prays here, before he is told to stop: the ban follows the prayer. He is not rebuked for praying. The ban itself is a form of the LORD's pain, since he says elsewhere that he has 'grown tired of relenting' (15:6).

echoes: Leviticus 26:19-20; Deuteronomy 11:13-17; Deuteronomy 18:20-22; 1 Kings 17-18; Hosea 8:13; Jeremiah 2:13; Jeremiah 6:14; Jeremiah 7:16; Jeremiah 8:15; Jeremiah 23:21; Lamentations 5:22; 2 Peter 3:4

settings.by: Jeremiah, in the form of a lament
settings.to: The people of Jerusalem and Judah, who are living through the dry season
settings.when: In a year of drought, undated
settings.why: To set before the people the picture of the land in mourning: the farmers, the nobles' servants, the animals, so that they see what the drought is and what sin has brought. It is the opening of a lament for the community.
settings.readers: Exiles who read it saw in the empty cisterns the other 'broken cisterns' of 2:13.

settings.by: The people, or Jeremiah praying for them
settings.to: The LORD, with the community listening
settings.when: At a fast in the drought
settings.why: To plead: sins confessed, but the LORD's name and presence among them given as the reason to act.
views: A prayer spoken by the community at a fast.
The prophet prays on behalf of the people, as Moses and Samuel did.

settings.by: The LORD, through Jeremiah
settings.to: Jeremiah, and through him the people
settings.when: In answer to the prayer
settings.why: To make clear that the time for turning aside the sentence has passed, and that fasts and offerings do not replace turning back.

settings.what: Jeremiah and the prophets of peace
settings.by: Jeremiah and the LORD, in dialogue
settings.to: Jeremiah, and the people who heard the prophets of peace
settings.when: In the same years
settings.why: To tell Jeremiah that the prophets who promise peace were not sent, so their word has no power, and that they and their hearers will be killed by the very things they deny.
settings.readers: The collected book gave the exiles the test by which to judge their own prophets (compare 29:8-9).

settings.by: The LORD tells Jeremiah what to say, and the speaker weeps
settings.to: The people
settings.when: During the drought and the war that follows
settings.why: To show that the one who announces the judgment weeps over it, so that no one can say the prophet is glad.

settings.by: The people, or Jeremiah praying for them
settings.to: The LORD
settings.when: At the same fast
settings.why: To ask once more not to be rejected, appealing to the LORD's name, his throne and his covenant, and to his power alone over the rain.

title: The First Complaint
sum: The LORD says that even Moses and Samuel could not turn him now. Judah will be sent to death, sword, famine and captivity, and nobody will pity Jerusalem. The mother of seven faints, and the widows outnumber the sand.

Then Jeremiah breaks in: 'Woe to me, my mother, that you gave birth to me.' He has eaten the LORD's words and found them sweet, but he sits alone, with a wound that will not heal. He accuses the LORD of being like a stream that fails. The LORD does not comfort him. He tells him to turn back, and promises to make him a bronze wall.
readings: Read as the prophet's honesty
The book lets Jeremiah say to God what pious people usually do not. His complaint is not a sin; it is the cost of the call.
Read as a test
The LORD's answer (15:19) is a call to repent. Jeremiah's prayer has crossed a line, and God corrects him, as he will not correct the psalmists. The faithful prophet has to be kept faithful.

views.H: 15:4 puts the cause of the disaster in the reign of Manasseh, and 15:1-9 describes the coming defeat. The confession belongs to Jehoiakim's years, when Jeremiah met open hostility.
views.C: 15:1-4 is prose, 15:5-9 poetry, 15:10-21 the first of the confessions as it stands here (the first is 11:18-12:6). The Greek has the text of 15:11-14 in a very different form, and 17:3-4 repeats 15:13-14. Several critics argue that verses 15:12-14 are later or misplaced. The mention of Manasseh in 15:4 is thought by many to be an editor's, to bring Jeremiah in line with Kings.
views.J: Jewish readers take 15:1 as the standard of intercession: Moses and Samuel are the two greatest pleaders (Psalm 99:6 names them with Aaron among those who called on the LORD), and even they would not help now. Ezekiel 14:14 makes the same point with Noah, Daniel and Job.
views.X: Christians have seen Jeremiah as a type of the suffering righteous one and of Christ rejected by his own. The eating of the words (15:16) is echoed in Revelation 10.
views.F: Some futurists read 15:12 'iron from the north' as the end-time northern power; most readers take the verse as about Babylon.

deep.b:
Five poems (11:18-12:6; 15:10-21; 17:12-18; 18:18-23; 20:7-18) interrupt Jeremiah's preaching to show him praying, or arguing, with God. They are the nearest the Bible comes to a prophet's diary. They begin as laments in the style of the Psalms: complaint, cry for revenge, a statement of trust. They differ from the Psalms because they are tied to a particular man and his history, and because God answers (12:5-6; 15:19-21) and does not always comfort. The label 'confessions' does not mean confessing sins; it means opening the heart. The speaker may be Jeremiah or a stylized voice, and the book is open about both.

Reading them in order gives a story: a man who begins sure of the LORD (11:18-20), asks why the wicked prosper (12:1-4), is told it will get worse (12:5), accuses God of unreliability (15:18), is told to turn back (15:19), asks for revenge (17:18; 18:21-23), and finally curses the day he was born (20:14-18). The story does not end in peace.

echoes: Exodus 32:11-14; 1 Samuel 12:19-23; Psalm 99:6; Ezekiel 14:14; Jeremiah 1:9; Jeremiah 1:18-19; Jeremiah 17:3-4; Revelation 13:10; Revelation 10:9-10

settings.by: The LORD, to Jeremiah, to tell the people
settings.to: The people of Jerusalem and Judah, who ask 'Where shall we go?'
settings.when: After the drought liturgy of chapter 14
settings.why: To make known that the decision is final: four fates, four destroyers, and no one to pity. Manasseh's old sins are named as the cause, to show that the judgment is the settling of an old account as well as a response to the present.
views: A message of the prophet under Jehoiakim.
15:4 is added to make the text fit the Deuteronomistic account in Kings.

settings.by: Jeremiah, to the LORD
settings.to: The LORD; later readers overhear
settings.when: During the years of opposition under Jehoiakim
settings.why: To bring his anguish to God: he is hated for the message, he is alone, and the LORD seems to have failed him. For readers it shows that the prophet's cost was real.
settings.readers: The exiles, who had suffered what Jeremiah had foretold, could see in his protest their own questions to God.

settings.by: The LORD, to Jeremiah
settings.to: Jeremiah
settings.when: In answer to the complaint
settings.why: To call him back to the task and to promise protection: he must return, speak what is precious and not worthless, and he will stand like a bronze wall.

title: No Wife, No Funeral, No Feast
sum: Jeremiah is forbidden three ordinary things: to marry and have children, to join a house of mourning, and to join a house of feasting. Each is a sign. Children born in this land will die of disease and lie unburied, there will be no mourners to cut themselves and no cup of comfort, and the voices of the bridegroom and bride will fall silent.

When the people ask why, Jeremiah is to tell them: they and their ancestors served other gods. Yet a promise breaks in: the day will come when no one swears by the Exodus, but by the God who brought Israel back from the north. The chapter ends with a prayer in which the nations come to the LORD from the ends of the earth and admit that their gods were nothing.
readings: Read as signs
Each prohibition is a sign for the community. A man without a family and without friends at funerals and feasts shows what is coming for everyone.
Read as part of the prophet's cost
The signs are also the price Jeremiah pays. He is made lonely, as the confession of 15:17 says, so that his life matches his message.

views.H: The signs belong to the years before 597 BC. The hunter and fisher threats were fulfilled in the deportations of 597 and 586 BC and in the hunting of fugitives (compare 2 Kings 25:4-7).
views.C: 16:10-13 is in the style of the book's prose sermons and is thought by many to be the work of later editors shaped by Deuteronomy. 16:14-15 repeats 23:7-8 and is usually seen as an editorial promise added to a chapter of doom, and 16:19-21 as a later prayer. The Greek lacks 16:5's 'loyal love and compassion' and 16:6's first two sentences (see the variants).
views.J: Jewish readers have read the chapter as grief and consolation together: the silence of the wedding voices is answered by the promise of a new exodus. Jeremiah 16:19-17:14 is the prophetic reading (haftarah) read with the Torah portion Bechukotai (Leviticus 26-27), which contains the covenant blessings and curses.
views.X: Christians have heard 16:16 in Jesus' call to be fishers of people (Mark 1:17) and 16:19-21 as a promise of the gospel to the nations. 1 Corinthians 7:26-29 gives the nearest New Testament parallel to the prophet's single life.
views.F: Some readers take 16:14-15 as still to be fulfilled in a final regathering of Israel; others take it as fulfilled in the return from Babylon, and others as fulfilled in Christ and the church.

deep.b: Marriage and children were taken for granted in Israel; childlessness was a misfortune. Jeremiah's life is made childless as a sign, because children born in these years would grow up to die. Neither the Jewish nor the Christian tradition has made this a rule for all; both read it as an exception for one man at one time. In Christian history the verse has sometimes been cited in discussion of celibacy, but the New Testament's own reasons for celibacy are the kingdom of God (Matthew 19:12) and the 'present distress' (1 Corinthians 7:26), not Jeremiah.

echoes: Leviticus 19:28; Deuteronomy 14:1; Deuteronomy 28:26; Jeremiah 7:34; Jeremiah 23:7-8; Isaiah 43:16-19; Mark 1:17; Revelation 18:23; 1 Corinthians 7:26-29

settings.what: Three commands for the prophet's life
settings.by: The LORD, to Jeremiah
settings.to: Jeremiah, and through him the people of Jerusalem who would see his life
settings.when: Undated; before the first deportation of 597 BC
settings.why: To make Jeremiah's household a sign: no wife and children, no mourning rites, no feasts, because the whole community is coming to the point where all these will stop.
settings.readers: The exiles knew the signs had come true: those years had no weddings or proper burials.

settings.by: The LORD, to Jeremiah, to tell the people
settings.to: The people who ask 'What is our guilt?'
settings.when: When Jeremiah explains the signs
settings.why: To give the reason in the covenant's terms: their ancestors left the LORD and served other gods, and the present generation has done worse.
views: A sermon of the prophet in Deuteronomy's language.
The Deuteronomistic editors compose the explanation, as in 5:19 and 22:8-9.

settings.what: A new exodus, and fishers and hunters
settings.by: The LORD, through Jeremiah
settings.to: The hearers in Judah, and the exiles who later read the book
settings.when: A promise set in the middle of judgment; the same promise is in 23:7-8
settings.why: To say that the judgment is not the end: the LORD will bring his people back from the north. First he will find them wherever they hide.
settings.readers: For the exiles in Babylon this verse was the promise that their journey would be reversed.

settings.by: Jeremiah, to the LORD
settings.to: The LORD, with future readers overhearing
settings.when: Undated
settings.why: To look past the judgment to a day when the nations see that the gods of their ancestors were nothing, and know the LORD's name.

title: Two Trees and the Sabbath Gates
sum: Judah's sin is cut into the heart and the altars with an iron pen. Then comes a poem of two ways: cursed is the one who trusts in people, like a shrub in the salt desert, and blessed the one who trusts in the LORD, like a tree by water that does not fear a dry year. Between them stands the line that has been quoted for centuries: the heart is crooked and sick beyond healing, and who can know it? The LORD says he does.

Jeremiah prays for healing and complains of mockers. The second half is a sermon at the city gates: carry no load on the sabbath. If the people obey, the city will stand forever, with kings in chariots and worshipers from all the land; if not, a fire will burn the fortresses of Jerusalem.
readings: Read as a pair of poems and a sermon
17:1-4 is a verdict, 17:5-11 a wisdom poem, 17:12-18 a prayer, and 17:19-27 a sermon. They are held together by the heart, the water and the fire.
Read as the story of one man's heart
The chapter moves from the sin on Judah's heart, through the question 'who can know it?', to the prophet's own heart open before God (17:16), and to the people whose hearts ignore the sabbath.

views.H: The sabbath sermon is addressed to Jehoiakim's or Zedekiah's reign. The promise of kings riding in chariots was not met, and the fire came in 586 BC (39:8; 52:13). After the exile Nehemiah applied the same teaching at the gates (Nehemiah 13:15-22).
views.C: 17:1-4 is absent from the Greek and repeats 15:13-14. 17:5-8 is close to Psalm 1. 17:19-27 is in the prose style of the book's sermons, and many critics see it as written or reworked after the exile, when the sabbath became a mark of Jewish identity. The conditional promise to the Davidic kings is thought by some to be a later hope. Others accept the sermon as Jeremiah's own.
views.J: Jewish readers see the sermon as proof that the sabbath was already a central test in the First Temple period. The Mishnah (Shabbat 7:2) lists carrying from one domain to another among the thirty-nine kinds of work; that law is later than Jeremiah and rests on its own reasoning. Jeremiah 16:19-17:14 is read as the haftarah with Bechukotai.
views.X: The two trees are paired with Psalm 1 in Christian preaching. 17:9 is used for the doctrine of original sin (see the card). Jesus' 'the sabbath was made for humans' (Mark 2:27) is read against the sermon by some, as an answer to a rule that had grown very strict.
views.F: Few readers find the sabbath sermon still to come; some dispensational readers connect the promise of an enduring Jerusalem (17:25) to a future kingdom.

deep.b: In the Hebrew way of thinking the heart (lev) is the center of thinking and choosing, not only of feeling; the kidneys (kelayot) are the hidden seat of conscience. 'Crooked' is 'aqov, from the same root as Jacob's name, 'the heel-grabber': a heart that grabs and twists. The line that follows it (17:10) is the LORD's own: only he searches the heart. The context is a set of verses about trusting in humans and about wealth gained by injustice (17:11), and about the sin written on the heart (17:1). It describes Judah. Whether it also describes every human being is the subject of the card below.

Jeremiah's sermon is one of the longest sabbath texts outside the Torah (Nehemiah 13:15-22 and Isaiah 58:13-14 are comparable). It says three things: the sabbath is a day of rest for everyone, not a day of trading; keeping it is tied to the survival of the dynasty and the city; and the ancestors were commanded to keep it (17:22). It does not list every kind of forbidden work; it names carrying loads, which the rabbis later developed. The teaching was probably much in mind when Nehemiah posted guards at the gates (Nehemiah 13:19-22). Christians have disagreed about whether the sabbath binds them, and how (see the card).

The Greek has no 17:1-4. It reads 'deep' and 'man' where the Hebrew has 'crooked' and 'incurable' in 17:9, and 'fear' for 'see' in 17:8. It has 'the gates of the sons of your people' in 17:19. Where the Dead Sea scroll 4QJer-a is preserved (from 17:8) it follows the longer type of text, with small differences of spelling. See the variants.

echoes: Psalm 1:1-3; Job 19:24; Deuteronomy 28:1-68; Leviticus 4:7; Exodus 20:8-11; Nehemiah 13:15-22; Amos 8:5; Jeremiah 2:13; Jeremiah 11:20; Jeremiah 31:33; John 4:10-14; John 8:6; Revelation 2:23

settings.what: The verdict of the iron pen
settings.by: The LORD, through Jeremiah
settings.to: Judah and Jerusalem, 'my mountain in the open country'
settings.when: Undated; the passage is absent from the Greek, so it may have been added in the longer edition
settings.why: To say that the sin is permanent, cut into stone: it is engraved on the heart and on the altar horns, and the result is loss of land and slavery to enemies.

settings.by: The LORD, through Jeremiah, in the form of a wisdom poem
settings.to: Judah's kings and people, who were looking to Egypt and to alliances; later, any reader
settings.when: Undated; the political crisis of Jehoiakim's time is often assumed
settings.why: To put the choice plainly: trust in people (flesh) brings a dry life, and trust in the LORD a deep root. In its first setting the verse is about Judah's heart; whether it also describes every human heart is the subject of the card below.
settings.readers: The exiles, cut off from the land, read the tree by the water as a promise that they could still live in a dry year.

settings.by: Jeremiah, to the LORD
settings.to: The LORD; with the people mocking him in the background (17:15)
settings.when: In the years when Jeremiah's word seemed not to come true
settings.why: To ask for healing and protection, to say that he did not wish the disaster, and to ask that his enemies be shamed.

settings.what: The sabbath sermon at the gates
settings.by: The LORD, to Jeremiah, to be spoken at the gates
settings.to: The kings of Judah, all Judah and all who live in Jerusalem, as they come through the gates (17:20)
settings.when: Undated; usually put in the reign of Jehoiakim or Zedekiah; some critics date it after 586 BC
settings.why: To get the whole city, from the king down, to stop carrying loads on the sabbath, and to say that the dynasty and city stand or fall on it. The sabbath was the sign of the covenant and a test of whether the people would listen.
settings.readers: After the exile Nehemiah closed the gates on sabbath for the same reason, which shows how the passage was read.
views: A real address at the gates in the years before 597 BC.
A sermon shaped by editors or written after the exile, when the sabbath was a mark of Jewish identity.

traditions.q: Do Christians have to keep the sabbath, and on which day?
views: Yes, on the seventh day, Saturday. The sabbath is part of the unchanging moral law and a sign of creation and rest in Christ (Fundamental Belief 20).

The fourth commandment still binds, with the day changed to the first day of the week in honor of the resurrection; the whole day is to be kept holy, in worship and rest (Westminster Confession 21.7-8).

Sunday, the Lord's Day, replaces the sabbath as the day of rest and worship; the obligation rests on the Church's authority and the Lord's resurrection, not on the old law of the seventh day (Catechism of the Catholic Church 2174-2176, 2190-2191).

The sabbath as a fixed day was part of the law for Israel and is not binding on Christians; what remains is the commandment to set time apart to hear God's word (Luther, Large Catechism, the Third Commandment).
The Lord's Day is a day of rest and worship, observed on the first day of the week, according to the conscience of each believer (Baptist Faith and Message 2000, article VIII).

traditions.q: Does 'the heart is crooked and sick beyond healing' teach that human nature is wholly corrupt?
views: Yes, in the sense that every part of the person is touched by sin and the person is unable to do any spiritual good; this is taught from many texts, among them Jeremiah 17:9 (Westminster Confession 6.4; Canons of Dort III-IV, 1-4).
Original sin is a deep corruption of the whole nature and leaves no power to love God above all things (Augsburg Confession II; Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration I).
Original sin wounds human nature and inclines us to sin, but does not leave it totally corrupt; free will is weakened, not destroyed (Catechism of the Catholic Church 405-406).
Humans inherit death and a tendency to sin from Adam's fall (ancestral sin), but not Adam's guilt, and the image of God is not destroyed.

Humans are 'very far gone from original righteousness' and inclined to evil, but God's prevenient grace restores to everyone the ability to respond (Wesley, The Doctrine of Original Sin; Methodist Articles of Religion VII).

title: The Potter's House
sum: The LORD sends Jeremiah to a potter's workshop. A pot goes wrong on the wheel, and the potter simply makes another. The LORD says Israel is in his hands as clay in the potter's, and then states the rule behind the picture: when he threatens a nation and it turns from its evil, he changes his mind; when he promises a nation good and it does evil, he changes his mind about that, too. So the people of Judah are told to turn back.

They answer that it is no use. The LORD asks the nations if anyone has heard of such a thing, and compares the people's forgetfulness to the snow and streams that never fail. Then comes a plot against Jeremiah, and his fourth complaint, a prayer for revenge on those who dug a pit for him.
readings: Read as the freedom of God
The potter does what he likes. This is how Isaiah 45:9 and Romans 9:20-21 use the picture, and it stresses God's right over his creatures.
Read as the openness of God
Here the picture is turned: the potter can reshape the pot. The point is that the LORD's plans for nations depend on their response, which is the lesson 18:7-10 states outright.

views.H: The visit to the potter and the oracle fit the years before 597 BC. The plot of 18:18 comes from the officials and religious leaders who feared Jeremiah's word, and the pit he mentions anticipates the cistern of chapter 38.
views.C: 18:1-6 is the sign-act, in Jeremiah's own voice; 18:7-10 is a general principle, and many critics think it comes from the later editors, who like to state rules of this kind (compare 12:14-17; 26:3, 13). 18:13-17 is a poem that may have been placed here because of its words about forgetting the ancient paths. 18:18-23 is the fourth confession. The Greek and a Qumran copy differ in two places (see the variants).
views.J: Jewish readers take 18:7-10 as the rule that the LORD's decree is always open to repentance, the lesson of Jonah.
views.X: Christians take the potter as God's sovereignty (Romans 9:20-21), and also as his patience with a spoiled pot; Reformed and Arminian readers disagree about the balance (see the card). Others read 18:7-10 as the model for how prophecy of judgment works.
views.F: The potter's work with Israel is sometimes used by futurist readers for Israel's restoration after the church age; the more usual reading finds it fulfilled in the exile and return.

deep.b: 18:7-10 is the plainest statement in the Bible of a God who responds. The word nicham (relent, change his mind) is used of God here and in Exodus 32:14 and Jonah 3:10. Other texts say he does not change his mind (Numbers 23:19; 1 Samuel 15:29). Aquinas and Calvin held that God does not change, so that texts about his relenting speak the way humans speak. Others, such as Fretheim, hold that the texts mean what they say: the LORD is moved by the people's response, and his plans for them depend on it. Jewish tradition reads the verses as a principle of repentance. The note on 18:8 gives the details.

Chapters 18 and 19 are read together. In 18 the clay is soft and the potter can remake the pot; in 19 the jar is fired and, once smashed, cannot be mended. Some interpreters see a shift in time: the offer of 18:7-10 is open until a certain moment, and then it is closed. Others read the two pictures as two sides of one God, who both offers and judges.

echoes: Isaiah 29:16; Isaiah 45:9; Isaiah 64:8; Sirach 36:13; Romans 9:20-21; Jeremiah 1:10; Jeremiah 6:16; Jeremiah 26:3; Jeremiah 26:13; Jonah 3:10; Psalm 35:12; Psalm 109:4-5

settings.by: The LORD, to Jeremiah, in a sign he sees
settings.to: Jeremiah, then the people of Judah and Jerusalem
settings.when: Undated; a visit to a potter's workshop in Jerusalem
settings.why: To teach, from clay, that the LORD's plans for a nation are open to its response: threat can be withdrawn if the nation turns, and promise can be withdrawn if it does evil. The people are called to turn back while there is time.
settings.readers: The exiles read it as a promise that the exile need not be the last word, since the same potter can remake the pot (compare 24:6; 31:4).
views: 18:7-10 states the rule for all of the LORD's words about nations.
The emphasis is on God's right to do as he will (Romans 9).

settings.by: The LORD, through Jeremiah
settings.to: The people of Judah
settings.when: Undated
settings.why: To shame them: the nations have never heard of a people who forgot their God, while snow and streams keep faith with the places they belong to. They have left the ancient paths and will be scattered.

settings.by: The plotters speak (18:18); then Jeremiah, to the LORD (18:19-23)
settings.to: The LORD, with the plotters and later readers overhearing
settings.when: After the sign at the potter's house; the plot is by those who have heard his sermons
settings.why: The plotters want to silence Jeremiah by words, because they think they have enough teaching, counsel and prophecy of their own. Jeremiah's prayer asks the LORD to act: it shows how deep his hurt was.

traditions.q: Does the potter and the clay mean that God chooses some people for salvation and not others?
views: Yes. God freely chooses those he will save, before they have done anything, as a potter makes some vessels for honor; Romans 9 draws on this picture (Westminster Confession 3.3-7; Canons of Dort I).

No. Jeremiah 18:7-10 shows that God's dealings depend on how people respond; Romans 9 speaks of God's right to use nations and to choose a way of salvation, but he elects in view of faith (Wesley, Predestination Calmly Considered).
God wills all to be saved and predestines no one to hell; predestination to glory rests on his foreknowledge and grace (Catechism of the Catholic Church 600, 1037).
God elects in Christ those who will be saved, but does not elect anyone to damnation; the cause of damnation is unbelief (Formula of Concord, Solid Declaration XI).
God foreknows who will respond, and his grace works with human freedom; he does not make anyone for destruction (John of Damascus, Exact Exposition of the Orthodox Faith 2.30).

title: The Broken Jar at Topheth
sum: Jeremiah buys a clay jar and takes some of the elders of the people and some of the senior priests to the Valley of Ben-hinnom, to the entrance of the Potsherd Gate. There he speaks the LORD's words: the place has been made foreign, filled with the blood of the innocent, and used to burn children to Baal. It will be called the Valley of Slaughter. The LORD will 'empty out' the plans of Judah, as the jar is emptied, and the siege will be so terrible that people eat their children.

Then Jeremiah smashes the jar before the witnesses and says that the LORD will break this people and city as a potter's vessel is broken, past mending. He returns to the Temple court and repeats the message to the people, in a short form that sets up the next scene with Pashhur.
readings: Read as a sign-act with a sermon
The jar is the sign, the Hinnom valley the stage, the elders the witnesses. The words and the act belong together.
Read as the fall of the Temple and city
Topheth is a place of death; the city will be made 'like Topheth'. The chapter is a preview of 586 BC, when the fire fell and the siege starved the people.

views.H: The valley south of the city, the Potsherd Gate and the elders fit Jehoiakim's reign. The fall of the city in 586 BC brought the siege famine (Lamentations 4:10).
views.C: Critics ask whether 19:1-13 and 19:14-15 come from the same source. 19:3-9 is close to 7:31-34 and 32:35; the Greek lacks some phrases (see the variants). Chapter 19 is often thought to be a story told about Jeremiah (the biographical prose) that joins chapter 20.
views.J: The Valley of Hinnom (Gei Hinnom) later gave its name, Gehinnom, to the place of punishment after death in Jewish writing. The Ninth of Av is the fast that mourns the destruction of the Temple.
views.X: Christians relate the valley to Gehenna in Jesus' words (Matthew 5:22; 10:28; Mark 9:43-48). Matthew's account of the potter's field bought with Judas' money (Matthew 27:3-10) combines Jeremiah and Zechariah; it mentions Jeremiah, perhaps because of chapters 18, 19 and 32.
views.F: Few find this chapter still to come; the valley's later use as a picture of final judgment (Gehenna) is the nearest the future reading gets.

deep.h: Topheth and the burning of children
deep.b: The valley south of Jerusalem was a place where children were burned in the fire in the last decades of the kingdom. Jeremiah says it three times (7:31; 19:5; 32:35). The Torah forbids giving a child to Molech (Leviticus 18:21; 20:2-5); 2 Kings 23:10 tells how Josiah defiled the place. Some scholars have argued that the practice was a dedication in which children were passed through fire and lived, but Jeremiah's own words say burning, and Ezekiel says the children were killed (Ezekiel 16:21). The 'tophets' of Carthage held the burned remains of infants and animals; whether they show sacrifice or the burial of those who died young is still debated, and the debate is not settled. The name 'Gehenna' for the place of punishment comes from this valley.

deep.h: Wordplay: the jar and the emptying
deep.b: The jar (baqbuq) makes a gurgling sound when emptied. Jeremiah says the LORD will 'empty out' (baqoti) the plans of Judah. The sound of the jar and the verb are the same. It is an example of how the signs were heard as well as seen.

The Greek lacks 'as burnt offerings to Baal' (19:5) and the last sentence of 19:11 about burying in Topheth. It gives the valley as 'the burial ground of the sons of their children' (polyandrion) and renders Topheth by a Greek word, 'the fall' (diaptosis). 19:1 lacks 'elders of' before 'the priests'. 4QJer-a has the start of 19:1, and 4QJer-c part of 19:8-9; both agree with the Masoretic Text.

echoes: Leviticus 18:21; Leviticus 26:29; Deuteronomy 28:53-57; 2 Kings 23:10; 2 Chronicles 28:3; Jeremiah 7:31-34; Jeremiah 18:4; Jeremiah 32:35; Lamentations 4:10; Matthew 5:22; Matthew 27:3-10; Mark 9:43-48

settings.by: The LORD, to Jeremiah; Jeremiah acts and speaks
settings.to: The elders of the people and senior priests who went with him; the kings of Judah and the people of Jerusalem he addresses (19:3)
settings.when: Undated; a scene in the Valley of Ben-hinnom at the Potsherd Gate, probably in Jehoiakim's reign
settings.why: To make leaders, who would later have to answer for the disaster, witnesses to the warning: the city will be smashed past mending, as the jar is. The sign is for the elders and priests who saw it, so that they cannot say they were not told.
settings.readers: Exiles reading the story knew what the elders could not: that the valley and city fell.

settings.what: The short message in the Temple court
settings.by: Jeremiah, speaking for the LORD
settings.to: All the people gathered in the court of the LORD's house
settings.when: After coming back from Topheth
settings.why: To say publicly in the Temple, where it will be heard by Pashhur, that the disaster will come on the city and its towns, because the people will not listen.

title: Terror all around
sum: Pashhur, the priest in charge of order at the Temple, hears Jeremiah and has him beaten and put in the stocks. In the morning Jeremiah gives him a new name, Terror all around, and says he and his friends will die in Babylon, to which all Judah will be taken.

Then the book gives its rawest prayers. Jeremiah says the LORD enticed him and won; the word of the LORD has made him a laughingstock. He tried not to speak, but it burned like a fire in his bones. His friends wait for him to stumble. A sudden hymn of trust stands between this and the last poem, in which Jeremiah curses the day he was born and asks why he came out of the womb at all.
readings: Read as the climax of the confessions
The five poems end here, with praise (20:13) and then with the darkest curse. There is no answer from the LORD, and the book moves on.
Read as a pair with Job 3
The curse on the day of birth links Jeremiah with Job. Both are men who lose their sense of the meaning of their lives, and neither is rebuked for the words.

views.H: Pashhur's arrest of Jeremiah is a conflict between priestly authority and the prophet, probably in Jehoiakim's reign (609-598 BC), when Jeremiah's preaching in the Temple (7; 26) angered the priests. Pashhur's prophecy of exile was fulfilled for the people of Judah in 597 and 586 BC; the book does not report Pashhur's death in Babylon.
views.C: 20:1-6 is part of the narrative stories about Jeremiah; 20:7-18 is the last confession. Some see 20:14-18 as separate from 20:7-13 and as a late composition in the manner of Job 3. The Greek differs in the name (20:3, see the variants) and lacks details of the plunder in 20:5.
views.J: Rashi (as given in the Sefaria text) reads 20:7 as 'You enticed me to go on your mission', and on 'you were stronger than I' adds 'you overcame me against my will'. Neither gloss reads it as a charge of cheating.
views.X: Christians have read Jeremiah as a type of the suffering Christ and have heard 20:9 in Paul's 'woe to me if I do not preach' (1 Corinthians 9:16).
views.F: Few read this chapter as future; the king of Babylon's coming is placed in 605-586 BC.

deep.b: The verb pittah in 20:7 is a hard word to translate. It is used of persuading a person, of seducing a young woman and of a lying spirit sent to entice a king. The Greek has 'you deceived me', and so the English tradition has 'deceived'. The Plain says 'enticed', so that the same verb in 20:10 (his enemies hope he will be 'enticed') can be seen. The weight of the charge is that Jeremiah says the LORD talked him into a task he did not want and then used his greater strength. There is no reply in the text. The book lets the charge stand. Some interpreters hear sexual violence in the pair 'entice and overpower' (compare Deuteronomy 22:25-28); others hold that this reads too much into a verb of persuasion. The Plain does not decide.

Pashhur son of Immer is the first named opponent of Jeremiah in the book. The Temple's chief officer kept order; he was a priest of the line of Immer (1 Chronicles 24:14). His new name, Magor-missabib, 'Terror all around', is a play on his own name, perhaps an Egyptian name ('son of Horus'). A pun in the other direction is the Greek's: it gives 'Exile', as if the name were 'sojourner'. The man himself passes out of the story, but later Pashhurs appear in the book (21:1; 38:1).

echoes: Job 3:1-26; Psalm 31:13; Psalm 39:1-3; Amos 3:8; 1 Kings 22:20-22; Ezekiel 14:9; Jeremiah 1:5; Jeremiah 6:25; Jeremiah 11:20; Jeremiah 17:10; Jeremiah 29:26; 1 Corinthians 9:16; Genesis 19:24-25

settings.by: Pashhur strikes Jeremiah; Jeremiah answers him with the LORD's word
settings.to: Pashhur son of Immer, and his friends, in the Temple area
settings.when: Right after the sermon at Topheth, in the Temple courts; the next day when Jeremiah is released
settings.why: Pashhur wanted to silence the prophet; Jeremiah turns it into a sign, giving Pashhur a name and telling him that he and his friends will see the sword and go to Babylon to die.
settings.readers: The exiles knew that Babylon had come and Pashhur's confidence had failed.

settings.by: Jeremiah, to the LORD
settings.to: The LORD; later readers overhear
settings.when: After the night in the stocks, in the same crisis
settings.why: To tell God that the call has cost him everything, that he cannot stop speaking, and that his friends wait for him to fall; and then to say, against all this, that the LORD is with him like a warrior.
views: 20:7-13 is a single lament that ends in a hymn of trust.
The hymn in 20:13 is a fragment that breaks into the lament.

settings.what: The curse on the day of birth
settings.by: Jeremiah, in his own voice
settings.to: No one is addressed; the speaker curses a day and a man who is not there
settings.when: Undated; placed at the end of the confessions
settings.why: To give voice to total despair without a reply. It shows what is left when the prophet has lost everything. The book leaves it as the last of the confessions.
views: It was composed apart from 20:7-13 and joined to it by the editors.
